sections.heading: Seeing that every good thing leads back to you
sections.text: My God, you have been teaching me to see that every honor, every joy, and every good gift is only good because it comes from you. You can give these things, and you can take them away. Help me not to stop at the gift, but to see the Giver. You are the good behind every good thing.
theological_themes: God is the source of all goodness; created blessings are real but dependent on him; God’s gifts should lead the heart back to worship.

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every truly good gift comes from God, so gratitude for created blessings should rise beyond the blessing itself to the Father who gives it.
Job acknowledges God’s right both to give and to take away, which supports the prayer’s trust that gifts are not ultimate and remain under God’s wise rule.

sections.heading: Wanting your glory more than my comfort
sections.text: Teach me that true blessedness is not just receiving good things from you, or even enjoying good things in you, but showing your goodness, your beauty, and your worth through my life. It is astonishing that you would make a human life a place where your light can be seen—where you speak, act, fill, and shine through someone as weak as me.
theological_themes: The highest good is God’s glory; believers are called to reflect God’s character; God works through weak human creatures without making them divine.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls his people to live in such a way that others see their good works and give glory to the Father, matching the prayer’s desire to display God’s goodness rather than merely consume his gifts.
Paul describes God’s light shining in human hearts while emphasizing that the treasure is held in fragile vessels, which fits the prayer’s amazement that God would shine through a creature.

sections.heading: Being drawn to you as my only good
sections.text: Nothing is truly good apart from you. When I am near you, I am near everything I really need. To become like you is not a small improvement; it is glory. Let this be what pulls me forward—the deep attraction of knowing you, staying close to you, and being changed into your likeness.
theological_themes: God himself is the believer’s supreme good; nearness to God is better than lesser blessings; sanctification means being transformed into God’s likeness through Christ.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God is his portion and that nearness to God is his good, directly grounding the prayer’s claim that God himself is the believer’s greatest treasure.
Paul teaches that believers are transformed as they behold the Lord’s glory, supporting the prayer’s longing to be made like God rather than merely helped by him.

sections.heading: Trusting you in peace, trouble, and death
sections.text: You are all my good when life is quiet. You are my only support when trouble comes. And when my life here ends, you will still be enough for me. Help me believe this not only when I feel strong, but when everything else is stripped away.
theological_themes: God is sufficient in every condition; faith rests in God during peace, suffering, and death; the believer’s final hope is God himself.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm presents God as refuge and strength when the world feels unstable, which supports the prayer’s dependence on God in trouble.
The psalmist says that even when body and heart fail, God remains his strength and portion, matching the prayer’s confidence that God is sufficient at life’s end.

sections.heading: Receiving your will in every circumstance
sections.text: Help me see that your will is good in everything you allow and everything you command. When your will cuts across mine, teach me not to resent you, but to trust you and even be glad that your wisdom is better than my desires. Let me recognize you in warmth and fire, in daily food, and in every providence. Let me see your created gifts as your own hands reaching toward me and holding me.
theological_themes: God’s will is wise and good even when it conflicts with human preference; providence includes ordinary provision and hard circumstances; created things are instruments of God’s care, not replacements for him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul assures believers that God works all things together for good for those who love him, which supports the prayer’s trust that even unwelcome providences are governed by God’s good purpose.
Jesus submits his human desire to the Father’s will in Gethsemane, giving the clearest pattern for trusting God when obedience crosses what one naturally wants.
Paul teaches that created things can be received with thanksgiving because they are made good by God, which illuminates the prayer’s desire to meet God in ordinary gifts like food.

sections.heading: Giving myself and everything entrusted to me back to you
sections.text: You are the endless fountain of every good thing. Because I love you, I give myself back to you. Everything I have is already yours—my possessions, my family, my church, my body, my time, my whole self. Do with me, and with all you have entrusted to me, whatever will honor you most.
theological_themes: God owns all things; surrender is the fitting response to grace; possessions, relationships, and the self are entrusted to the believer for God’s glory.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers, in view of God’s mercy, to present themselves to God as living sacrifices, which grounds the prayer’s whole-person surrender.
Paul reminds Christians that they belong to God because they were bought with a price, supporting the prayer’s confession that the self is not finally self-owned.
David acknowledges that all offerings to God come from what God first gave, matching the prayer’s recognition that possessions and resources are already God’s.

sections.heading: Asking for comfort, but yielding to your wiser purpose
sections.text: If it fits your eternal counsel, your gracious purpose, and the great aim of your glory, please give me the comfort and encouragement I long for. But if your wiser decision is to withhold it, help me lay down my demand for comfort and trust you anyway. Your will is better than my preference, and your glory matters more than my ease.
theological_themes: Prayer asks boldly while submitting to God’s will; comfort is a good gift but not the highest good; God’s glory and wisdom govern what he gives or withholds.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches confidence in prayer according to God’s will, which supports the prayer’s request for comfort while submitting the outcome to God.
Paul pleaded for relief, but God gave sustaining grace instead; this fits the prayer’s willingness to receive either comfort or God’s wiser withholding.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about seeing “Deity in a creature” could be misunderstood as teaching that a human being becomes divine. I rendered it as God’s light, speech, action, and presence being displayed through a weak human life, preserving the sense of divine manifestation without implying ontological deification.

The line giving “my goods, family, church, self” to God can sound as though the person owns other people or the church. I kept the surrender but expressed family and church as realities entrusted to the person and belonging ultimately to God.

The prayer’s confidence that God’s will is good even when painful reflects a strong doctrine of providence. This can be pastorally sensitive in contexts of suffering, so the modern version keeps the claim without implying that evil itself is good or that grief is inappropriate.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “fire, and food and every providence” as including both ordinary created provision and harder circumstances, so the modern prayer says “warmth and fire, in daily food, and in every providence.”

I treated the prayer’s movement as: seeing God behind gifts, desiring God’s glory, being drawn to God as the only good, trusting him through all seasons, receiving providence, surrendering all, and submitting requests for comfort to God’s wisdom.
I kept the conditional request for comfort rather than turning it into a guaranteed expectation, because the original explicitly asks for comfort only if it serves God’s counsel, grace, and glory.
